results.title: What's Gone in macOS Golden Gate and What's Next in macOS 28
results.description: With macOS Golden Gate , Apple phased out several legacy features and services, cutting support for older devices and accessories. More cuts are coming in macOS 28 as Apple continues to root out lingering Intel features. Here's everything that's been dropped. Support for Intel Macs - macOS Golden Gate is the first version of macOS that runs only on Apple silicon Macs. Intel Macs can't run it and are limited to macOS Tahoe . Apple still plans to offer security updates through fall 2028. Boot Camp Assistant - Since macOS Golden Gate doesn't run on Intel Macs, it doesn't support Boot Camp. Apple silicon Macs require virtualization software like Parallels or VMware Fusion to run Windows. Rosetta 2 (Temporarily) - Upgrading to macOS Golden Gate removes Rosetta, but if you have an app installed that requires it, you can reinstall it. macOS Golden Gate is the last version of macOS that will have full Rosetta support. Apple Filing Protocol - Apple deprecated AFP back in macOS Sequoia 15.5, and there is no AFP client at all in macOS Golden Gate. Time Capsule Backups - With no support for AFP, Time Capsule no longer works with Macs running macOS Golden Gate. Time Capsule requires AFP or SMBv1, but Time Machine backups now use the SMBv2 or SMBv3 protocol. AirPort Utility - AirPort Utility is no longer included when you install macOS Golden Gate. If you had the app before updating, you can still use it, but Apple makes no guarantee that it still works. AirPort Utility lets users manage AirPort base stations like the AirPort Extreme and AirPort Express. macOS 28, which is expected in fall 2027, will largely drop support for Rosetta 2. Most apps that rely on Rosetta will not open on Macs running macOS 28, though Apple is making an exception for some legacy games that are unmaintained. In macOS Golden Gate, you'll see a warning when using any app that relies on Rosetta, so you're aware that the app won't continue to work in the future without a developer update. You can also see which apps are affected by going to Settings > General > About > Intel-Based Apps and then clicking on Details. results.title: Stocks mostly fall as oil prices and bond yields rise
results.description: Stock markets mostly fell and oil prices climbed on Thursday as US Treasury bond yields hit multi-year highs, driven partly by a lack of progress in ending the Middle East war. After a down day in Europe, Wall Street stocks began the session firmly in negative territory, but received a positive jolt around midday with a Reuters news agency report that Washington and Tehran had made headway on an accord to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. "It felt like that lasted for an hour-and-a-half," said B Riley Wealth Management's Art Hogan, adding that markets need greater evidence of concrete movement towards a deal. Stocks levelled off after the positive jump. The S&P 500 declined 0.02 percent to end the session at 7,704 points. The Nasdaq edged up 0.01 percent to 26,939 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.3 percent to 51,349 points. But the benchmark US 10-year Treasury yield rose to its highest level since 2007, and the 30-year yield reached its highest since 2004 as oil prices jumped. Japan's 10-year yield jumped to a 30-year high during Asia trading hours. "It is rare to get movements this volatile in sovereign bond markets, which is another sign that sovereign debt is going through an uncomfortable adjustment period," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. She pointed to a combination of rising governing debt loads and deficits, resilient economic growth and rising inflation risks. "These things together are anathema to the bond market and it is no surprise that yields are rising," she said. The rise in US yields also reflects solid economic data and rising expectations for additional tightening of monetary policy. Futures markets are betting with around 70 percent odds that the US Federal Reserve will increase interest rates in October. Such expectations drove 30-year US fixed-rate mortgages to more than 7.0 percent, a drag on consumers hoping to buy homes. Investors were also keeping an eye on the meeting between US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping at the White House. Few breakthroughs are expected during Xi's state visit. Instead the trip is more about the spectacle as the world's two biggest economies seek to manage points of friction. (AFP) Edited by Cecil Wong
